messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 69
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Plumber
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 35

He is a 69-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has worked most of his life as a plumber, a trade that once gave him pride because it kept him active, useful, and able to provide for his family. He is married now and speaks about his wife with a quiet protectiveness, as if she has long been the anchor that keeps him steady when his mind drifts into places he does not want to go.

The traumatic event happened many years ago, when he was much younger and still building his life in a place that never felt fully safe. He describes being taken captive during a period of political violence, held with other men in cramped quarters, and made to wait in a kind of helpless suspension that he remembers more clearly than the details of the building itself. He does not speak about the captivity with dramatic language. Instead, he says it in a low, matter-of-fact way, as though naming it plainly might keep it from swallowing him. What stays with him is the loss of control: the sound of doors locking, the uncertainty of when food would come, the way he learned to measure time by footsteps in the hall and the moods of the men guarding him.

In those days he learned to stay very still, to keep his face blank, and to watch everyone without appearing to watch. He remembers the heat, the smell of sweat and damp concrete, and the sharp awareness of his own body—his stomach knotted, his mouth dry, his muscles always ready to flinch. Even now, decades later, he can feel the old tension return when he is trapped in a small room or when he hears a heavy lock turn. He says there are moments in the present when his body reacts before his mind does, as if it has never fully accepted that he is free.

After he was released, he did what many men around him did: he went back to work. Plumbing suited him because it was practical and demanded focus. Pipes, fittings, leaks, and pressure gave him problems he could solve with his hands. For a long time, work helped him avoid thinking. He could kneel under a sink, crouched in a crawlspace, and be absorbed by the task. But even there, confined under houses or inside narrow utility rooms, he sometimes feels an old surge of panic that he has to hide from others. He has learned to excuse himself, to step outside, breathe slowly, and wait for his heart to settle before returning to the job.

He describes a life organized around vigilance. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He checks exits. He dislikes being surprised from behind. Loud banging, metal clanging, or sudden shouting can send a jolt through him that lingers for hours. Some nights he wakes with his chest tight and his mind full of the same unfinished fear he carried in captivity. He does not always remember a dream, only the sense that he has been somewhere bad and cannot get out. His wife says he talks in his sleep sometimes, and he is embarrassed by that, as if even in rest he cannot fully lower his guard.

He also notices that certain smells and temperatures pull him backward without warning. The damp smell of old basements, the taste of stale water, the sound of keys or padlocks can bring on a brief, vivid return of the past. In those moments, he does not simply remember what happened; he feels himself there again, tense and cornered, with a dread that is difficult to put into words. Afterwards he becomes tired and irritable, and he tends to withdraw. He is not a man who speaks easily about fear, so he often responds by becoming quieter, by working longer, by staying busy in the garage or fixing things around the house until the feeling passes.

Over time, he has become more aware of how much of his life is spent avoiding reminders. He will not watch films about war or imprisonment. He dislikes crowded gatherings where he cannot move freely. He says he loves his family deeply but sometimes feels distant even when he is with them, as though part of him is still standing watch somewhere else. At the same time, he shows tenderness in small, practical ways—repairing a dripping faucet before it becomes a problem, checking the locks at night, making sure his wife is comfortable before he is.

He presents as a man who has survived by endurance and discipline, but who still carries the captivity in his body and in the rhythms of his daily life. The years have not erased the experience so much as woven it into the way he moves through the world, alert to danger, careful with trust, and always prepared for the moment when something ordinary might suddenly feel like a trap.
